messages.subject: Integrated distance sampling models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

FYI, we just uploaded the pre-print of a paper in which we develop what we call integrated distance sampling, or IDS, models: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17229.

IDS models combine proper distance sampling data with distance-free point count or detection/nondetection data and enable estimation of a latent detection function for the distance-free data types. This achieves a reconciliation of the spatial mismatch between these data types. We also show how with extra-information (such as variable survey duration) one can estimate the parameters of an availability process. This then addresses the temporal mismatch that typically exists when one tries to combine such data from different surveys. To fit these models, we provide JAGS code and a new IDS() function in unmarked.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Post-hunting survival ~1 in two-season Brownie model
messages.subject_clean: Post-hunting survival ~1 in two-season Brownie model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am running a two-season Brownie band-recovery model with mallard data from the Atlantic, Mississippi and Central flyways in North America. We have banding data from pre-hunting season (Jul-Sep) and post-hunting season (Feb-Mar), and band-recovery data during the hunting season (Oct-Jan) and we'd like to estimate hunting season, post-hunting season, and annual survival probabilities under a Bayesian framework using jagsUI R package. We are basing our analysis on the model published by Devers et al. (2021) in Ecological Applications with some modifications. The timeframe of our analysis is 1991-2021 and we are estimating age-sex class-specific (i.e., juvenile male, juvenile female, adult male and adult female) survival probabilities with temporal variation.

The problem is when I ran the model, the post-hunting survival estimates are basically 1 for the majority of the years. I thought that might be because we don't have enough data to estimate age-sex specific survival, so I combined juvenile and adult data and tried to just estimate sex-specific instead. However, the resulting estimates are still very close to 1 except for the most recent years (see attached figure).

Does anyone have any idea why this might be happening? Is this a data issue or model issue (or both)? I am happy to provide the model code and R script (including data) if anyone's interested in taking a look, but possible explanations for why this is happening or advice on steps I can take to find out the root cause are all appreciated!

Thanks so much!
Angela

Angela Hsiung (she|her)
Postdoctoral Researcher

James C. Kennedy Waterfowl and Wetlands Conservation Center

Belle W. Baruch Institute of Coastal Ecology and Forest Science

Clemson University

messages.subject: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?
messages.subject_clean: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm working through some mark-recapture data for basic survival estimates and trying to add complexity with some variables of interest. In this dataset, we have sex, age, and categorical site data. When working through examples in the AHM and IPM books (which are incredibly helpful!) there's usually a note that you *can* add complexity with covariates but not really how to do that.

My goal is to get estimates of age class-specific survival across three different sites.

I ran it with the linear model looking like:
logit(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu <http://phi.mu> + beta.age*age[i,t] + beta.site2*site2[i] + beta.site3*site3[i]

Where age is an array of 0 = juvenile, 1 = adult and site2/3 are dummy variables, therefore phi.mu <http://phi.mu> is juvenile at site 1.

It technically works but the estimates aren't tracking with the prior model I ran to just get adult site-specific estimates (where I used site as the only predictor therefore the identity link).

So, with multiple categorical predictors, both time-dependent (age) and just individual-dependent (site doesn't change), is there a different way the linear model should be coded?

Alternatively, should I create a grouping variable, one for each of the six combinations (2 ages, 3 sites?) This  method is how I got site and sex specific survival when I used the adults only.

The bigger picture question I haven't found the answer to exactly is how JAGS understands when a 1, 2, 3 is group 1 etc., (as in, site[1]) as opposed to a numerical predictor value of 1, 2, or 3. Is this all in the choice of link in the linear model? Does adding more than one predictor automatically necessitate a logit or other link function?

Thanks in advance from a beleaguered recent MS grad who feels a bit out of her depth!

Stephanie

messages.subject: Re: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?
messages.subject_clean: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephanie,

> It technically works but the estimates aren't tracking with the prior model I ran to just get adult site-specific estimates (where I used site as the only predictor therefore the identity link).

I'm not exactly sure what you mean, but when you're adding any predictors at all, you should be using the logit-link. So even with just site, it should be:

logit(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu <http://phi.mu> +  beta.site2*site2[i] + beta.site3*site3[i]

Alternatively, and this gets to one of your other questions, if you have an (unordered) categorical predictor, you're essentially just estimating three intercepts. So you could formulate this as:

(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[site[i]],

where site[i] is a predictor variable taking on the values 1, 2, or 3 for the three sites. Each individual has its own site covariate so you get three indices in phi.mu <http://phi.mu>. The prior would be:

for (i in 1:n_site) {
   phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[i] ~ dlogis(0, 1)
}

Or some such.

> So, with multiple categorical predictors, both time-dependent (age) and just individual-dependent (site doesn't change), is there a different way the linear model should be coded?

If you want a separate estimate for each age * site combination, you could do:

logit(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[site[i],age[i,t]],  # actually, with this specification you don't need the logit link, because each probability is getting estimated separately!

where age[i,t] is a time-varying individual covariate (e.g., at time 1 it may be a juvenile "1" and at time t-1 it might be adult "2"). Then the prior becomes:

for (i in 1:n_site) {
   for (j in 1:n_age) {
      phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[i,j] ~ dlogis(0, 1)  # with logit-link
#      phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[i,j] ~ dbeta(1, 1)  # without logit-link

   }
}

> The bigger picture question I haven't found the answer to exactly is how JAGS understands when a 1, 2, 3 is group 1 etc., (as in, site[1]) as opposed to a numerical predictor value of 1, 2, or 3. Is this all in the choice of link in the linear model? Does adding more than one predictor automatically necessitate a logit or other link function?

I struggled to understand this for a while as well. JAGS doesn't know anything about what each number means; it's about how you code it. If you have beta * x[i] it fits a single coefficient through that cloud of predictors vs. response. If you index coefficients by the values therein, e.g., beta[x[i]], it estimates separate betas for each value of x. Does that make sense? Btw, there are other link functions available, but yes, you'll need a link function most of the time because you can't let the probabilities go outside of [0,1]. Another good link function is the loglog-link. This estimates your survival probabilities as mortality rates, which has many nice properties including being able to deal quite well with unequal time intervals in multistate models (see https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13059).

Hope this helps (and that I was correct).

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc,

Thanks for the words of encouragement and the suggestions. I’ll make sure I give that paper a good read. Seems like random sampling is a good route to go down.

Best wishes,

Chris

From: Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>
Date: Wednesday, 30 November 2022 at 16:23
To: 'Christopher Dean' <christophe...@gmail.com>, hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: AW: Dealing with uneven number of visits when using palaeontological data

Dear Dean,

thanks for your message. I find this a real fascinating application of occupancy models !

I think it makes sense to subsample your data to avoid an undue (?) influence of super-highly-sampled regions. This seems to common practice in occupancy modeling for citizen-science data, see this publication:  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ddi.13271, where they say this about their use of ebird data for fitting occupancy models: “Where there were more than 10 visits to a single site, we randomly selected 10 of the visits.”

Happy modeling !

Best regards -- Marc

Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> Im Auftrag von Christopher Dean
Gesendet: Mittwoch, 30. November 2022 13:42
An: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Betreff: Dealing with uneven number of visits when using palaeontological data

Hi everyone,

Apologies for anyone in the unmarked group for the crosspost - just posting in here to cover my bases. I’m also going to preface this by saying I’m very new to occupancy modelling in general, so apologies if there is a simple answer to this!

To give some background, I’m a palaeontologist who’s become interested in occupancy modelling as a way to better understand the factors influencing preservation in the fossil record. In my current project, I’m attempting to apply some single season occupancy models to a dataset of dinosaur occurrences from the end Cretaceous using unmarked to answer questions about how the fossil record influences perceived patterns prior to the end Cretaceous mass extinction at 66 million years ago. Asides from a few papers, occupancy modelling hasn’t really caught on in palaeo yet, so I’m unsure about how to setup my data considering the peculiarities of fossil data.

In terms of my setup, I’ve downloaded North American fossil occurrences from the paleobiology database (http://paleobiodb.org for those interested), which contains presence only records of fossil occurrences reported in ‘collections’ (basically a collecting event from a distinct rock horizon/geologic time at a specific geographic locality). Collections can have one or many fossils occurrences within them. I have then used R to grid up collections from the same time intervals into both 0.1 or 0.5 degree grids, with the aim of testing these datasets in different occupancy models. I am using these grid cells as my ‘sites’, and then each collection is a ‘visit’, with the presence of my target taxon within each collection as a detection, and the absence of it as a non-detection. This is similar to how I’ve seen some occupancy approaches deal with historical data not specifically collected for occupancy modelling, and also similar to some other palaeo papers that have used occupancy modelling.

However, my issue comes with the fact that I have a strongly uneven number of visits between sites, which is introducing an enormous amount of NAs in the site by species matrix. To give an example, the majority of my sites (grid cells) have between 1-3 collections in them, but maybe 5% of them have between 80-130 collections. This obviously is extremely skewed, and I’ve read elsewhere that having such uneven numbers of visits can cause problems for the model through the introduction of NAs. As such, I’ve been trying to decide on a way to deal with it, and I’ve come up with a number of options:
Leave it, and accept that this might cause issues (definitely not my preferred method!).
Truncation of sites. There’s a paper (Lawing, A.M., Blois, J.L., Maguire, K.C., Goring, S.J., Wang, Y. and McGuire, J.L., 2021. Occupancy models reveal regional differences in detectability and improve relative abundance estimations in fossil pollen assemblages. Quaternary Science Reviews, 253, p.106747) that’s applied occupancy modelling to fossil pollen records, which also had issues with uneven ‘visits’ between ‘sites’ (although their setup differed from mine due to their data types). To deal with this, they introduced a cut off of 10 ‘visits’, and removed any further visits from their matrix. They found that this improved model results, but I was somewhat unsure of the validity of removing any visits after the first 10 or so.
Remove those sites. Another possibility would just be removing any sites which have a vastly larger number of visits. However, fossil data is already fairly sparce, and I would then be losing a large amount of potentially valuable information.
Subsample/make ‘average’ occupancy. My final thought was to effectively create an ‘average’ detection history. I wrote a quick script in R that randomly samples the detection history of a site with more visits than a specified limit (e.g. 10 visits per site) 1000 times to generate an ‘average’ detection history. However, this obviously means I can’t attach observation level detection covariates within this model. I also thought about randomly sampling a specific number of visits and just running the model, but then each model would have to be run many times to create an ‘average’, and interpreting the results from that would be very problematic.

As you can see, I am unsure of the best procedure to use, or whether any of these options make sense. I am also unsure of whether this is a also indicative of a larger issue of spatial auto-correction, and whether that should be incorporated in my model somehow.

Does anyone have any suggestions or thoughts on what the best course of action for me may be?

Thanks so much for reading (sorry this ended up so long!), and if you have any questions just let me know and I’ll do my best to clarify for you!

Best wishes,

Chris

messages.subject: point transect distance sampling in JAGS (problem with AHM1 code)
messages.subject_clean: point transect distance sampling in JAGS (problem with AHM1 code)
messages.body_plain:
hi all,

We have discovered an important problem in AHM1 and AHM2 with the way in which we fit Bayesian distance sampling models for point counts. This problem concerns the model of Section 8.3.4 of AHM1 and all subsequent sections that deal with point counts (or "point transects") for binned data.

In short, the use of the rectangular approximation to the integral used to obtain probability of capture (and to define distance class probabilities) doesn't work so well when there are very coarse intervals (and/or very few intervals, because they must get coarser as you reduce the number of intervals!). We noticed this problem when we had a situation with distance intervals (0, 25m), (25, 50), (50, 75), (75, 100) and (100, 500) with sigma = 100 or so. For this situation there was extreme bias introduced in the estimates of sigma and density. This is not an intrinsic problem of having coarse intervals but rather is due to the way the BUGS model was formulated, where the cell probabilities were based on the prescribed coarse distance classes. This can be resolved by reformulating the BUGS model a little bit. Instead of using the prescribed (too coarse) intervals to define the interval probabilities, the interval probabilities should be computed  within the BUGS model specification by using a FINER choice of distance bins, and then aggregating/summing up these smaller pieces to match the observed distance classes. We provide a script with comments below that shows how to do this.

In retrospect, this is an obvious limitation of the formulation given in the AHM books, and we apologize for any problems that it caused (or analyzes that have to be re-done...).

regards,
andy

library(AHMbook)
library(jagsUI)

simout<- NULL

# Simulate 1000 cases. This takes 30 minutes or longer.
for(sim in 1:1000){

# Use the sim.pdata function from AHMbook to simulate a data set with distances recorded out to 500 m (B=5)
B<- 5
rm(tmp)

N.true<- 3000  # To get very large sample sizes
sigma.true<- 1
tmp <- sim.pdata(N=N.true, sigma=sigma.true, keep.all=FALSE, B=B)
attach(tmp)

D.true<- N.true/((2*B)^2)   # because the simulator simulates locations on a square

# Define distance intervals, mid-points and interval widths
 xg<- c(0, .25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 5)
 midpt <- c(0.25/2, 0.25 + 0.25/2, 0.5 + 0.25/2, 0.75 + 0.25/2, 3)
 delta<- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 4)
# convert observed distances into numerical index for distance class
 dclass<- as.numeric(cut(d, breaks= xg))
 table(dclass)

nD <- length(midpt) # how many intervals
nind <- length(dclass) # how many individuals were detected

# Bundle and summarize data set

# First we re-define an alternative set of interval properties that will be used to compute the cell probabilities.
# In this case we use a constant interval width of 0.25 and so there are 20 such intervals:
 midpt2 <- seq(0.25/2, 5-0.25/2, 0.25)
 delta2<- rep(0.25, length(midpt2))
 nD2<- length(midpt2)

# The finer resolution intervals are fed into JAGS instead of the prescribed ones used for data collection
str( win.data <- list(midpt=midpt2, delta=delta2, B=B, nind=nind, nD=nD2, dclass=dclass) )

# BUGS model specification, conditional cell probabilities version
cat("
model{
# Prior for single parameter
sigma ~ dunif(0, 10)  # must be changed depending on spatial scaling

# Construct cell probabilities for nD cells (rectangle approximation)
#
# This loop computes the integrand at the midpoint of a rectangle for each of nD rectangles.
# nD should be largerish and it is NOT equal to the number of observed distance classes
# but, rather, should be large enough to get a good approximation to the probability of detection.
# Unsure what that is but 20 is probably ok, 10 might be ok, 5 is probably not ok.
#
for(g in 1:nD ){ # midpt[g] = midpoint of each distance band
 log(p[g]) <- -midpt[g] * midpt[g] / (2*sigma*sigma)
 pi[g] <- (( 2 * midpt[g] ) / (B*B)) * delta[g]
 f[g] <- p[g] * pi[g]
 fc[g] <- f[g] / pcap
}
pcap <- sum(f[]) # capture prob. is the sum of all rectangular areas. The rectangular approximation to the integral has to estimate this quantity with sufficient precision

# Now here we aggregate the probabilities based on the rectangular evaluations into the
# observed (prescribed) distance classes. In this case the first 4 map 1:1 to the observed
# distance classes because they are all 0.25 units, and the last one goes from 1 to 5 units
# so it is the sum of all probabilities from 5 to nD.

# Distance class probabilities based on aggregation: (with fancy BUGS coding you could avoid hard-wiring this in)
fc2[1]<- fc[1]
fc2[2]<- fc[2]
fc2[3]<- fc[3]
fc2[4]<- fc[4]
fc2[5]<- sum(fc[5:nD ])

# Categorical observation model
for(i in 1:nind){
  dclass[i] ~ dcat(fc2[])
}
# Derived quantities: population size and density
  N <- nind / pcap
  D <- N/(3.141*B*B)
}

",fill=TRUE, file="model3.txt")
# Inits function
inits <- function(){list (sigma=runif(1, 1, 10)) }
# Params to save
params <- c("sigma", "N","D")
# MCMC settings
ni <-  2000 ; nb <- 1000 ; nt <- 2 ; nc <- 3
# Run BUGS and summarize posteriors

out3<- jags(win.data, inits, params, "model3.txt", n.adapt=500, n.chains = nc,
 n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, n.thin = nt, parallel = TRUE)

print(out3)

simout<- rbind(simout, c(out3$mean$sigma,out3$mean$D) )
}

apply(simout,2,mean)

rel.bias<- apply(simout,2,mean)/c(sigma.true, D.true)

messages.subject: Weird class-specific population size estimates in IPM
messages.subject_clean: Weird class-specific population size estimates in IPM
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Huge thanks to those who offered helpful insight to my last question about the two-season Brownie model! The Brownie model is working, but I now have a different issue. The Brownie model is the survival submodel of an integrated population model for mallards. The IPM contains a dead-recovery model, productivity submodel that estimates juvenile:adult age-ratio using wing data from USFWS, and a population count submodel using the Waterfowl Breeding Population and Habitat Survey population estimates (divided by 10,000) as data. We are estimating both overall breeding population and age-sex class-specific population sizes using a matrix model within the IPM.

My problem now is that, while the overall population estimates from the IPM seem to follow the data (WBPHS estimates) fairly closely, the class-specific population sizes have some weird patterns (see attached figures). Specifically, while juvenile and adult male populations seem to increase over time, both juvenile and adult female populations decrease to almost 0, which doesn't seem realistic. I have tried adjusting the priors for the observation error component of the population count model, as well as priors for the initial population for each cohort. However, the same pattern still persists.

Again, if anybody has any guesses for why we are seeing these results, and/or has advice on how to diagnose this problem, I'm all ears! I am also happy to share the code and/or model output if needed.

Thank you!
Angela

messages.body_plain:
Hey Ramiro,

Just thinking out loud here. Currently you're estimating the covariances separately for each year, even though you might want to model the sigmas and rhos in Sigma <- diag(sigma) %*% Rho %*% diag(sigma) hierarchically, right?

This will be a pain if you have many species, but you could do something like:

Omega[1:nspec,1:nspec,t]<- inverse(Sigma2[1:nspec,1:nspec,t])  # covariance to precision matrix
Sigma2[1:nspec,1:nspec,t] <- diag(sigma[1:nspec,t]) %*% Rho[1:nspec,1:nspec,t] %*% diag(sigma[1:nspec,t])  # decompose covariance into sigmas and Rho
## define Rho somewhere; this'll be a pain depending on how many species there are, but something like
Rho[1,1,t] <- 1
Rho[1,2,t] <- rho[1,t]
Rho[1,3,t] <- rho[1,t] * rho[2,t]  # not even sure if this would be the correct cell entry, but you get where I'm going?

# hierarchical sigmas (log-transformed)

for (s in 1:nspec) {

   log(sigma[s,t]) ~ dnorm(sigma_mu[s], sigma_tau[s])
}

# hierarchical rho's
for (j in 1:nrho) {
   rho[j,t] <- (exp(2 * rho_fz) - 1) / (exp(2 * rho_fz) + 1)  # need to do inverse Fisher's z-transform to go from [-∞,∞] back to [-1,1]
   rho_fz[j,t] ~ dnorm(rho_fz_mu[j], rho_fz_tau[j])  # need to do the random year effects on unbounded scale (Fisher's z-transform)
}

and then place priors on sigma_mu[1:nspec], sigma_tau[1:nspec], rho_fz_mu[1:nrho], and rho_fz_tau[1:nrho].

Cheers,

Matt
